IndustroEquip Holdings - Q2 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the IndustroEquip Holdings Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. If you're using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss IndustroEquip Holdings' results for the second quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson.

Sarah Thompson (CEO):
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on IndustroEquip Holdings' performance for the second quarter of 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts despite a challenging macroeconomic environment, delivering solid results through disciplined execution and strategic focus in our core industrial equipment business, which spans CNC machining centers, automated material handling systems, precision robotics, and heavy-duty hydraulic presses.

First, we've navigated macroeconomic headwinds effectively, with global PMI contraction pressuring demand but selective bright spots in electrification, reshoring, and aerospace helping us outperform peers. Our book-to-bill held relatively steady, and backlog provides good visibility. Second, our cost reduction initiatives have driven substantial profitability improvements, with gross margins expanding meaningfully through supply chain optimization, operational excellence, and overhead discipline. Third, revenue performance varied by geography, with North America showing resilience from infrastructure and onshoring tailwinds, offsetting softer Europe and mixed Asia. Finally, our M&A activity continues to sharpen our portfolio, with recent deals enhancing our automation capabilities and regional footprints.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Michael Chen to provide more detail on our financial results.

Michael Chen (CFO):
Thank you, Sarah. Turning to our financial performance, IndustroEquip Holdings reported $2.8 billion in revenue for the second quarter, representing a 2% increase year-over-year on an organic basis. Gross margin expanded to 31.6%, a 320 basis point improvement, driven by our cost actions and pricing discipline. Operating expenses were controlled at $720 million, resulting in operating income of $450 million. Our net income for the quarter was $280 million, or $1.42 adjusted EPS per share, up 8% year-over-year.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are committed to investing in our business to drive future growth and shareholder value.

As we dive deeper into our results, I'd like to spend some time on a critical topic: the impact of macroeconomic factors on our end market demand. As a leader in industrial equipment—spanning CNC machining centers, automated material handling systems, precision robotics, and heavy-duty hydraulic presses—our business is inherently cyclical and tied to capex cycles across manufacturing OEMs. While we've delivered this solid quarter, the macro headwinds have tempered demand growth to just 2% organically.

Let me break this down systematically, starting with the big-picture trends. Global PMI readings averaged 49.2 in Q2, signaling contraction for the fourth straight quarter, per ISM and S&P Global data. This has directly pressured our book-to-bill ratio, which slipped to 0.98x from 1.05x a year ago, reflecting softer quoting activity and delayed orders. End market demand across our portfolio declined 4% year-over-year, with backlog growth stalling at flat sequentially. But it's not all downside—selective bright spots in electrification and reshoring have helped us outperform peers like Caterpillar and Deere, whose industrial segments saw 6-8% drops.

The elephant in the room remains elevated interest rates. With the Fed funds rate at 5.25-5.50% and ECB rates at 4.25%, corporate borrowing costs have surged 200-300 basis points since 2022. This has led to widespread capex rationing among our OEM customers. For instance, in automotive, where we supply stamping presses and assembly line robotics, demand fell 12% YoY as Tier 1 suppliers like Magna and Lear deferred expansions amid high debt servicing costs. Our automotive segment, 22% of revenue, saw orders down 15%, with utilization rates at customer plants dipping below 75%—well off the 85% breakeven threshold.

Conversely, in sectors less sensitive to rates, we've seen resilience. Aerospace and defense, 18% of our mix, grew 9% on the back of Boeing and Airbus ramp-ups for narrow-body jets like the 737 MAX and A320neo. Our backlog here jumped 22% to $1.2 billion, fueled by aftermarket MRO equipment demand.

Persistent inflation, hovering at 3.2% globally per IMF estimates, has compounded this. Raw material costs—steel, aluminum, and copper—rose 7% QoQ despite some easing, squeezing margins and delaying projects. Our semiconductor end market, which relies on precision wafer fab equipment akin to Applied Materials' offerings, contracted 18% due to inventory destocking and softening consumer electronics demand. Chipmakers like TSMC and Intel have pushed out fab expansions, with our book-to-bill here at a dismal 0.85x.

Energy prices add another layer. Brent crude at $82/barrel and European natural gas still 40% above pre-Ukraine levels have hit oil & gas and chemicals. Our energy segment (15% of revenue) was flat YoY, as upstream drillers like ExxonMobil prioritized cash flow over rig upgrades. However, we've captured share in LNG infrastructure, with orders up 25% for compressor skids and heat exchangers.

Regionally, the picture is bifurcated: North America (52% of revenue) was relatively resilient at +1% demand growth, buoyed by the IIJA infrastructure bill and CHIPS Act. Factory utilization hit 78%, per Fed data, supporting construction equipment demand up 5%. Reshoring trends are a tailwind—our U.S. robotics orders surged 14% as automakers build battery gigafactories, mirroring Tesla's Texas expansion. Europe (28%) was the weakest link, down 11% YoY. The energy crisis post-Russia sanctions has crushed manufacturing PMI to 45.8, with German autos idling lines. We've seen deferred orders for wind turbine nacelle tooling from Vestas and Siemens Gamesa, though our renewables sub-segment grew 8% on EU Green Deal subsidies. Asia-Pacific (15%) was a mixed bag. China, 9% of our total, plunged 20% amid property sector woes and youth unemployment at 15%. Stimulus hopes are fading, with CNC machine demand mirroring the 12% drop in fixed asset investment. Japan and Korea offset some pain, up 4%, driven by fab equipment for Samsung's HBM memory ramps. Rest of World (5%) saw emerging markets like India and Mexico gain 7%, fueled by nearshoring. Our Mexico facility is at 95% capacity, supplying EV press lines to BMW's San Luis Potosí plant.

We're not passive observers. Our strategy emphasizes diversification—reducing automotive exposure from 30% in 2020 to 22% today via M&A like our 2023 acquisition of RoboForge for collaborative robots. We've leaned into megatrends: Electrification and sustainability now tie to 35% of Q2 orders for EV/battery or renewables. Investments in our 'EquipGreen' platform—digital twins for energy-efficient presses—have won spec positions at Ford and Rivian, boosting win rates 15%. Amid labor shortages (U.S. manufacturing vacancies at 600k+), our AI-driven predictive maintenance suites, integrated with Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk, saw 28% uptake. This has stabilized aftermarket revenue at 42% of total, less cyclical than new equipment. We proactively built 1.5 months of channel inventory pre-2022 disruptions, now drawing it down to manage 8% YoY COGS inflation. Regionalization—adding capacity in Mexico and India—has cut lead times 20% and shielded against Red Sea shipping delays.

Looking ahead, we expect macro pressures to linger through H2, with global end market demand flat to down 2%. But our $4.1 billion backlog provides 7 quarters of visibility at current run rates, and we project 4-6% organic growth in FY25 as rates ease (Fed cuts by 75bps anticipated). Free cash flow remains robust at $450 million for the year, funding $300 million in buybacks and capex skewed to high-ROI digital initiatives. We're positioned defensively yet offensively in growth pockets like aero, renewables, and semis reshoring.

Now, turning to our cost reduction initiatives, which have been a cornerstone of our strategy this quarter and have delivered meaningful leverage to our profitability amid this challenging macroeconomic backdrop in the manufacturing and industrial equipment sector. As you know, we've been navigating headwinds like persistent inflation in key inputs—steel prices up 12% year-over-year, aluminum averaging $2,800 per metric ton, and logistics costs still 20% above pre-pandemic levels—while demand for our core products, including CNC machining centers, hydraulic presses, and automated assembly lines, remains soft in non-residential construction and OEM markets.

Our comprehensive cost actions generated $185 million in savings over the last 12 months, exceeding our initial $150 million target by 23%. This directly contributed to the 320 basis point expansion in gross margins from 28.4% in Q2 last year to 31.6% this quarter—our highest in five years. On an adjusted basis, EBITDA margins expanded 450 basis points to 16.2%, with operating income up 28% sequentially despite only 2% revenue growth. These aren't one-off cuts; they're structural improvements embedded in our operations, positioning us to outperform in the next upcycle, much like we saw peers such as Caterpillar and Deere achieve during the 2021 recovery.

Diving into the initiatives, our largest bucket—42% of total savings, or $78 million—came from supply chain optimization. We've consolidated our vendor base from 1,200 to 850 strategic suppliers, focusing on long-term contracts with pricing floors tied to LME indices for metals and Platts for energy. This reduced procurement costs by 9.2%, particularly for high-volume components like servo motors and precision gears. A key move was nearshoring 25% of our Asian-sourced castings and forgings to Mexico and Eastern Europe, cutting lead times by 35% and ocean freight exposure amid Red Sea disruptions. Regionally, this has been a game-changer in North America, where reshoring trends aligned with the CHIPS Act and IIJA have allowed us to pass through fewer tariff impacts—down to 1.5% of COGS from 4%—while Europe faced headwinds from the EU's CBAM carbon border taxes, which we mitigated via low-carbon steel blends from ArcelorMittal.

Next, operational excellence in our 28 global facilities accounted for 35% of savings, or $65 million. We've accelerated our Industry 4.0 rollout, deploying IoT-enabled predictive maintenance across 65% of our machining lines, reducing unplanned downtime by 22%—from 8% OEE loss to under 6.5%. For context, this mirrors Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk platform but customized for our heavy-duty equipment like our 500-ton stamping presses. Lean manufacturing kaizen events yielded another 4% labor productivity gain, with cross-training programs offsetting skilled labor shortages in the U.S. Midwest. Energy efficiency upgrades, including variable frequency drives on 1,200 compressors and LED retrofits, shaved 15% off utility bills, critical in Europe where natural gas prices spiked 40% post-Ukraine.

The remaining 23%, or $42 million, stemmed from SG&A discipline and overhead rationalization. We optimized our go-to-market model by digitizing 70% of our aftermarket parts ordering via a SAP S/4HANA platform, cutting order-to-cash cycles by 18 days and distribution costs by 11%. Workforce actions were measured—net headcount down 7% through attrition and redeployment, avoiding severance charges—and we clawed back $12 million in discretionary travel and consulting post our Q4 2023 review.

Regionally, North America drove 55% of savings, benefiting from stable energy costs and proximity sourcing, with gross margins hitting 34.2%. Asia-Pacific was flattish at 27% margins due to softer fab equipment demand amid semiconductor inventory builds at TSMC and Samsung, but our cost actions there preserved EBITDA at 14%. EMEA lagged at 29% margins, pressured by German energy costs, but our hedging—covering 80% of 2024 exposure—limited the hit to 50 basis points.

Strategically, these initiatives aren't just defensive; they're offensive plays for margin durability. We've de-risked our cost structure to a variable rate of 62% of sales, down from 68%, giving us pricing power as capex cycles turn—think data center builds boosting demand for our precision robotics arms, akin to the ABB and Fanuc surge in 2022. Sustainability ties in too: our Scope 1 and 2 emissions dropped 18% via electrification, aligning with customer ESG mandates from the likes of Boeing and GM.

Looking forward, we expect another $100 million in run-rate savings by year-end, with gross margins targeting 33% in 2025, even at flat volumes. This positions us to lap tough comps and deliver 20%+ EPS growth as industrial production indices recover—ISM PMI now at 48.5, but leading indicators like our book-to-bill at 1.15x signal inflection.

Shifting to revenue performance by geographic region, I'm particularly pleased to highlight how this totaled around our quarterly figure amid ongoing Industry 4.0 adoption and manufacturing reshoring trends. Excluding any one-time items, organic growth was solid at 9% in key areas. Book-to-bill remained healthy at 1.15x, with backlog at $4.1 billion overall, up from last year, providing strong visibility.

North America, roughly 52% of total revenue and our growth engine, delivered resilient results at +1% demand growth but with revenue surges fueled by onshoring under the CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act. Shipments to U.S.-based OEMs in automotive and semis increased notably, as customers prioritize domestic supply chains. Tailwinds from infrastructure spending boosted heavy-duty palletizers and conveyor systems. Our expanded facilities improved lead times, and aftermarket services saw strong uptake.

Europe, at 28%, faced a mixed picture with declines on constant currency due to FX and energy pressures, but we gained share in renewables with low-emission servo drives and major contracts for modular robotic arms. Challenges in autos and chemicals were offset by new assembly capacity in Poland reducing logistics costs.

Asia-Pacific, 15%, showed mixed resilience, led by India and Southeast Asia with explosive growth in infrastructure and electronics assembly. China softened due to real estate and overcapacity, but advancements in AI predictive maintenance secured business. Emerging markets like Vietnam offset headwinds.

Rest of World, 5%, grew on nearshoring in Mexico and steady Middle East aftermarket.

Overall, geographic diversification shielded us, with North America and emerging markets offsetting Europe. We're positioned in automation and sustainability, expecting regional growth acceleration in Q3.

Finally, on M&A activity and the strategic rationale driving it, this continues to be a cornerstone of our long-term value creation strategy as the leading provider of precision industrial equipment for metal forming, automation, and material handling. The sector navigates tailwinds like global reshoring from the U.S. CHIPS Act and IRA, Europe's Green Deal, and Asia's EV/renewables growth at 12-15% CAGR. Supply chain issues make bolt-on M&A essential for tech IP, footprints, and aftermarket—now 42-45% of recurring revenue.

In recent quarters including Q2 momentum, we closed transformative deals like the acquisition of a Germany-based leader in collaborative robotic welding and AI adaptive machining, bringing high-margin revenue and synergies through cross-selling and platform integration. This sharpened our automation portfolio, adding to EPS and positioning us strongly in EV battery and semis. We also divested legacy low-margin forging to unlock proceeds for repurchases and bolt-ons, contributing to segment growth.

Strategically, these de-risk our growth targets, bolstering Europe and U.S. ops for battery and fab pipelines. Our pipeline is robust at $2-3 billion, prioritizing digital enablers, APAC capacity, and sustainability, with LOIs signed and announcements expected. ROIC exceeds hurdles, fueling mid-teens EPS growth.

Q&A Session:

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question comes from Jennifer Hale with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Jennifer Hale (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the automotive market?

Sarah Thompson (CEO):
Good morning, Jennifer. Absolutely, automotive remains challenging at 22% of our mix, with orders down 15% YoY due to interest rate pressures and capex deferrals at Tier 1s like Magna. Utilization below 75% has led to delayed expansions, but we're mitigating through diversification—reducing exposure from 30% historically—and capturing EV opportunities. Reshoring in North America, like battery gigafactories, drove U.S. robotics up 14%, and our EquipGreen platform is winning specs at Ford and Rivian. We see stabilization as rates ease.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

David Patel (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Michael Chen (CFO):
Thanks, David. Our FY24 capex is targeted at around $450 million in free cash flow supporting $300 million total, skewed to high-ROI digital initiatives like Industry 4.0 and regional capacity. For FY25, we plan $200 million focused on Mexico, Poland, and digital twins for agility and margin expansion to 22%+. This includes nearshoring investments cutting lead times 35% and IoT predictive maintenance across more lines, aligning with peers like Rockwell. It's defensive for resilience but offensive for growth pockets like renewables and semis.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen (Morgan Stanley):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

Sarah Thompson (CEO):
Lisa, supply chain remains a focus, but our proactive steps are protecting margins. We built 1.5 months inventory pre-2022, now drawing down to handle 8% COGS inflation, and regionalized with Mexico/India capacity cutting lead times 20% against Red Sea delays. Nearshoring 25% of castings/forgings saved $78 million, reducing tariffs to 1.5% of COGS. Vendor consolidation to 850 suppliers with LME-tied contracts dropped procurement 9.2%. These, plus IoT reducing downtime 22%, drove our 320 bps gross margin expansion to 31.6% despite steel up 12% and logistics 20% elevated. Hedging covers 80% exposure, limiting hits.

Closing Remarks:

Sarah Thompson (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in IndustroEquip Holdings. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Alex Rivera (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
